{{Use American English|date = February 2019}}
{{Short description|Type of Borel measure}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Gaussian measure''' is a [[Borel measure]] on finite-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>, closely related to the [[normal distribution]] in [[statistics]]. There is also a generalization to infinite-dimensional spaces. Gaussian measures are named after the [[Germany|German]] [[mathematician]] [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]]. One reason why Gaussian measures are so ubiquitous in probability theory is the [[central limit theorem]]. Loosely speaking, it states that if a random variable <math>X</math> is obtained by summing a large number <math>N</math> of independent random variables with variance 1, then <math>X</math> has variance <math>N</math> and its law is approximately Gaussian.

==Definitions==
Let <math>n \in N</math> and let <math>B_0(\mathbb{R}^n)</math> denote the [[complete measure|completion]] of the [[Borel sigma algebra|Borel <math>\sigma</math>-algebra]] on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>. Let <math>\lambda^n : B_0(\mathbb{R}^n) \to [0, +\infty]</math> denote the usual <math>n</math>-dimensional [[Lebesgue measure]]. Then the '''standard Gaussian measure''' <math>\gamma^n : B_0(\mathbb{R}^n) \to [0, 1]</math> is defined by
<math display="block">\gamma^{n} (A) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}^{n}} \int_{A} \exp \left( - \frac{1}{2} \left\| x \right\|_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}^{2} \right) \, \mathrm{d} \lambda^{n} (x)</math>
for any measurable set <math>A \in B_0(\mathbb{R}^n)</math>. In terms of the [[Radon–Nikodym derivative]],
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d} \gamma^{n}}{\mathrm{d} \lambda^{n}} (x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}^{n}} \exp \left( - \frac{1}{2} \left\| x \right\|_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}^{2} \right).</math>

More generally, the Gaussian measure with [[mean]] <math>\mu \in \mathbb{R}^n</math> and [[variance]] <math>\sigma^2 > 0</math> is given by
<math display="block">\gamma_{\mu, \sigma^{2}}^{n} (A) := \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^{2}}^{n}} \int_{A} \exp \left( - \frac{1}{2 \sigma^{2}} \left\| x - \mu \right\|_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}^{2} \right) \, \mathrm{d} \lambda^{n} (x).</math>

Gaussian measures with mean <math>\mu = 0</math> are known as '''centered Gaussian measures'''.

The [[Dirac measure]] <math>\delta_\mu</math> is the [[weak convergence of measures|weak limit]] of <math>\gamma_{\mu, \sigma^{2}}^{n}</math> as <math>\sigma \to 0</math>, and is considered to be a '''degenerate Gaussian measure'''; in contrast, Gaussian measures with finite, non-zero variance are called '''non-degenerate Gaussian measures'''.

==Properties==
The standard Gaussian measure <math>\gamma^n</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>
* is a [[Borel measure]] (in fact, as remarked above, it is defined on the completion of the Borel sigma algebra, which is a finer structure);
* is [[Equivalence (measure theory)|equivalent]] to Lebesgue measure: <math>\lambda^{n} \ll \gamma^n \ll \lambda^n</math>, where <math>\ll</math> stands for [[absolute continuity#Absolute_continuity_of_measures | absolute continuity]] of measures;
* is [[Support (measure theory)|supported]] on all of Euclidean space: <math>\operatorname{supp}(\gamma^n) = \mathbb{R}^n</math>;
* is a [[probability measure]] <math>(\gamma^n(\mathbb{R}^n) = 1)</math>, and so it is [[Locally finite measure|locally finite]];
* is [[Strictly positive measure|strictly positive]]: every non-empty [[open set]] has positive measure;
* is [[Inner regular measure|inner regular]]: for all Borel sets <math>A</math>, <math display="block">\gamma^n (A) = \sup \{ \gamma^n (K) \mid K \subseteq A, K \text{ is compact} \},</math> so Gaussian measure is a [[Radon measure]];
* is not [[Translation (geometry)|translation]]-[[Invariant (mathematics)|invariant]], but does satisfy the relation <math display="block"> \frac{\mathrm{d} (T_h)_{*} (\gamma^n)}{\mathrm{d} \gamma^n} (x) = \exp \left( \langle h, x \rangle_{\R^n} - \frac{1}{2} \| h \|_{\R^n}^2 \right),</math> where the [[derivative]] on the left-hand side is the [[Radon–Nikodym derivative]], and <math>(T_h)_*(\gamma^n)</math> is the [[pushforward measure|push forward]] of standard Gaussian measure by the translation map <math>T_h : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n</math>, <math>T_h(x) = x + h</math>;
* is the probability measure associated to a [[normal distribution|normal]] [[probability distribution]]: <math display="block">Z \sim \operatorname{Normal} (\mu, \sigma^2) \implies \mathbb{P} (Z \in A) = \gamma_{\mu, \sigma^2}^n (A).</math>

==Infinite-dimensional spaces==
It can be shown that [[There is no infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure|there is no analogue of Lebesgue measure]] on an infinite-dimensional [[vector space]]. Even so, it is possible to define Gaussian measures on infinite-dimensional spaces, the main example being the [[abstract Wiener space]] construction. A Borel measure <math>\gamma</math> on a [[separable space|separable]] [[Banach space]] <math>E</math> is said to be a '''non-degenerate (centered) Gaussian measure''' if, for every [[linear functional]] <math>L \in E^*</math> except <math>L = 0</math>, the [[push-forward measure]] <math>L_*(\gamma)</math> is a non-degenerate (centered) Gaussian measure on <math>\mathbb{R}</math> in the sense defined above.

For example, [[Classical Wiener space|classical Wiener measure]] on the space of [[continuous function|continuous]] [[path (topology)|paths]] is a Gaussian measure.
